1.pericope_label: Where is the bill of your mother’s divorcement: the tongue of the learned, and the back given to the smiters

schools.summary: Read the questions as implying their own negative answers, refuse to narrow the divine coming to one occasion, assign the soliloquy to the Servant while allowing echoes of the prophet, and render the tongue and ear in the vocabulary of the schoolroom.

Deny the prophetic reference outright against the Jewish commentators, offer several referents at once for the darkened heavens, and hear in the opened ear the bored ear of a servant who would not go free.

Insist the chapter speaks more clearly of Jesus of Nazareth than of the son of Amos, collect the manuscript evidence, and assemble the eastern usage that makes plucking the beard and spitting the gravest indignities.
Work both questions as points of law, so that the writ must be produced and the creditor named, and draw the ministerial moral that none should teach who have not first learned.

debates.question: Who speaks from the fourth verse onward?

positions.view: not the prophet at all, against Aben Ezra, Kimchi and others who hold it
the chapter has been understood of the prophet, but it speaks more clearly of Jesus of Nazareth than of the son of Amos
the prophet says something of himself and then, like David, speaks of himself as a type
the prophet in some sort, but the words are far more eminently verified in Christ and seem meant directly of him
the Servant in an abruptly introduced soliloquy, not Isaiah, though echoes of the prophet's own experience may legitimately be traced
the one in whom God had come to his nation and proclaimed the way of salvation

debates.question: What is proved by the missing bill of divorcement and the absent creditor?

positions.view: that the writ would have been put into the woman's own hand, and that God was in debt to none of the powers they were sold to, so the separation is their own doing
that this wife was never formally repudiated as her sister had been, and that no creditor among the nations could claim her children
that God is neither governed by such motives nor urged by such necessity, so the captivity is to be imputed to their own folly
that the scope of this discourse and the next is to vindicate God's justice and convict them of causing their own calamities

debates.question: What does the darkening of the heavens refer to?

positions.view: the darkness in Egypt, or ordinary tempest and eclipse, or the darkness at the crucifixion, all at once
thick and dark clouds interposed, which God balances
a covering black as sackcloth drawn when a people must be saved
one item in a piling up of mighty works whose sequence recalls the plagues of Egypt
part of the answer to the charge that the hand is shortened, following the radical sin of disobedience to the word

outliers.reading: Alone hears the morning waking as a deliberate contrast with the dreams and night visions of a less perfect inspiration, and suggests the Gospel's early risings may be a conscious fulfilment of it.

Alone notes that the word for a disciple stands at both ends of the verse, an instance of the mirrored arrangement favoured throughout the book, and that it is the older form of the later term for pupils.

themes: Thus saith the Lord, Where is the bill of your mother’s divorcement, whom I have put away? or which of my creditors is it to whom I have sold you? Behold, for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves, and for your transgressions is your mother put away.

Wherefore, when I came, was there no man? when I called, was there none to answer? Is my hand shortened at all, that it cannot redeem? or have I no power to deliver? behold, at my rebuke I dry up the sea, I make the rivers a wilderness: their fish stinketh, because there is no water, and dieth for thirst.
I clothe the heavens with blackness, and I make sackcloth their covering.

The Lord God hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary: he wakeneth morning by morning, he wakeneth mine ear to hear as the learned.
The Lord God hath opened mine ear, and I was not rebellious, neither turned away back.
I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting.

7.pericope_label: My face like a flint: who is he that shall condemn me, and the fire of your own kindling

schools.summary: Rest the whole confidence on one support, render the adversary as the master of a lawsuit, hear in the darkness what every true servant knows, and keep both received senses of the kindled fire.

Guard the promise of help against misuse by referring it to the human nature, locate the vindication in resurrection and ascension, and read the fire as reason, tradition or self-righteousness put up in place of the given light.

Protest that the verse about walking in darkness has been dangerously misread, adopt Lowth's redistribution into two questions with two answers, and offer general, particular and pastoral senses for the fire.
Describe the believer in the dark from the inside, evidences clouded and comfort suspended, and set against him the man who offers sacrifice with fire of his own striking.

debates.question: Can one who truly fears God walk in darkness without light?

positions.view: no, and the common reading is dangerous; the verse holds two separate questions with two separate answers, as Lowth divides it and the Greek and Syriac support
yes, and the case is described from the inside — evidences clouded, joy interrupted, the Spirit's testimony suspended, the light of God's countenance eclipsed
yes, and every true servant knows it, the cry of dereliction being the extreme case and the commending of the spirit the answering trust
yes, provided the darkness is understood as misery and not as sin
the question is put so that whoever can answer to it may learn what he is to do
the fear in question is filial and not slavish, and those who have it are always few

debates.question: What is the fire that men kindle for themselves?

positions.view: their own righteousness, sacrifice offered with fire of their own striking rather than fire from heaven, and worldly comforts as short-lived sparks
human devices and worldly policy generally; or, with Vitringa, the factions who stirred up the war that burned their own city; or the presumptuous who think it criminal to doubt their salvation
any human substitute for the divine light, taking in both man's fiery wrath and his resting in earthly comforts, with some rendering the clause as girding oneself with firebrands
the light of nature and reason, or the traditions of men, or one's own righteousness, set up by those who reject the light of the world

debates.question: How is the vindication of the Servant secured?

positions.view: by forensic opposites, one verb declaring righteous and the other guilty, with the accusers already carrying the germ of their own destruction
by appeal from unrighteous earthly judges to one who judges righteously, so that the prosecutor ceases to matter
by events — the resurrection, the ascension, and the gifts poured out afterwards
by many and mighty signs clearing him publicly, the accused being conscious of his own innocency

outliers.reading: Alone protests that the verse has been quoted and preached on to prove a man may fear God, obey the Servant's voice and still have no sense of approbation, calls that impossible, and adds that where some write bitter things against themselves under a morbid melancholy the word of God should not be bent down to their state.

Alone stops to guard the promise of help against a christological objection, arguing that the words are spoken of the Redeemer as man, weak in that nature and crucified through weakness, so that the need for help proves the greatness of the work rather than any lack in his deity.

themes: For the Lord God will help me; therefore shall I not be confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be ashamed.
He is near that justifieth me; who will contend with me? let us stand together: who is mine adversary? let him come near to me.
Behold, the Lord God will help me; who is he that shall condemn me? lo, they all shall wax old as a garment; the moth shall eat them up.
Who is among you that feareth the Lord, that obeyeth the voice of his servant, that walketh in darkness, and hath no light? let him trust in the name of the Lord, and stay upon his God.

Behold, all ye that kindle a fire, that compass yourselves about with sparks: walk in the light of your fire, and in the sparks that ye have kindled. This shall ye have of mine hand; ye shall lie down in sorrow.
